quiz.reason: Supported. Editors may want the opioid point (card 21) nearby, so that 'not slow breathing and tiny pupils' is never read as 'not an overdose' in someone who used meth.
Passes: the Fact leans partly on the tentative one-of-three-periods finding, and 'if anything' carries that hedge.
Supported. The second why sentence mentions 'yearly death counts', which this card never shows; it is accurate but could be dropped.

item.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than teens who don't.
item.why: Combining three studies on thoughts and three on attempts, a review found about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and 3.5 times the odds of attempts in teens who used the most. That can't show cause: in other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were counted.

quiz.reason: 'A review of three studies each found' reads as if each study found these odds; they are pooled figures. Why reworded, statement unchanged.

item.statement: Mild serotonin syndrome is easy to tell apart from ordinary drug effects.
item.why: Mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects; doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, sweating and restlessness, and, when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever. A checklist of these signs was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses.

quiz.reason: Nobody believes or argues the original statement, and it is just a slice of its own why. The lines' 'mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects' gives a real myth that is useful for safety.
True and supported, but a dry trend line rather than something people argue about. Its forum-useful point (opioids in most of these deaths) is card 21, from the same claim.
Supported. Optional: the lines' coroner figure (about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there were using alone) is the safety point a why could carry.
'MAOI' is not in the lines, which say 'this kind of antidepressant'. The label is correct for moclobemide, so the card is fine if the editor accepts it.
True and supported, but an obvious Fact nobody argues about. The useful part (passing dark thoughts limited to the crash) is only in the why.

item.statement: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in children with Dravet syndrome, a form of epilepsy.
item.why: Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children on it, against 26 to 27 in 100 on a dummy liquid. But the maker ran both trials, in its own backup checks the result didn't always hold up, and shop CBD wasn't tested.

quiz.reason: A trick: the Myth turns on 43 to 49 in 100 falling just short of 'most', while the lines' finding is that the medicine beat the dummy. Rewritten as that finding, plus the forum-useful 'shop CBD wasn't tested'; 'severe', which the lines don't say, is dropped.

item.statement: In sleep labs, people who stopped heavy cannabis use got more dream sleep in the first nights.
item.why: They also slept less and took longer to fall asleep. That's from three small studies, two of them from the 1970s, and the data cover only the first week after stopping, so how long it lasts isn't known.

quiz.reason: The why gave the wrong reason why nobody knows how long it lasts: the lines say it is because the data cover only the first week, not because the studies were few or old. The statement is kept ('heavy' rests on the lines' 'very strong lab doses').
